analysis.one_liner: Establishes a nationwide right to IVF and requires insurance, Medicaid, Medicare, and military plans to cover fertility treatment.
analysis.headline: H.R. 9643, introduced in September 2024 with three Democratic cosponsors, was referred to six House committees and died without a hearing, markup, or vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal right for patients to get fertility treatment, including in vitro fertilization, and for providers to offer it, overriding state laws that restrict IVF or the handling of embryos. It would require employer and private health plans that cover maternity care to also cover fertility treatment without extra cost-sharing, and would add fertility coverage to Medicaid, Medicare, federal employee plans, and care for service members and veterans. It received only referrals to committees and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People trying to have children through fertility treatment, especially the many who pay five-figure out-of-pocket costs per IVF cycle because their insurance does not cover it. Also veterans and active-duty service members whose injuries or hazardous assignments affect fertility, same-sex couples and single parents who are often excluded by infertility-diagnosis requirements, and federal employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: IVF patients, veterans, and military families

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal statutory right for individuals to receive fertility treatment — including IVF, artificial insemination, embryo genetic testing, and preservation of eggs, sperm, and embryos — and for providers to offer it, superseding state laws that conflict with those rights.

Requires any group health plan or insurer that covers obstetrical services to also cover fertility treatment regardless of whether the patient has an infertility diagnosis, and bars cost-sharing for it that exceeds what the plan applies to other medical services.
Adds fertility treatment as a covered service under state Medicaid plans and under Medicare, with the deductible waived for fertility treatment.

Requires the Defense Department and the VA to furnish fertility treatment and counseling to service members and enrolled veterans and their spouses, partners, and gestational surrogates — without regard to sex, marital status, or infertility diagnosis — including up to three egg retrievals and unlimited embryo transfers, free fertility preservation and storage for members deploying to combat or hazardous duty, and reimbursement for donor material.
Adds fertility treatment benefits to the Federal Employees Health Benefits program for federal workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and insurers would bear the cost of the newly required benefit, passed on through premiums. States would bear added Medicaid costs, and the federal government added Medicare, defense, and VA costs. States that restrict the handling or disposal of embryos would lose that authority to federal preemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, insurers, states, and federal budgets

drawbacks.text: The coverage mandate applies to every group plan that covers obstetrical services and caps cost-sharing at the plan's usual level, a real added claims cost for employers and insurers that would flow into premiums for all enrollees.

Title I supersedes any inconsistent state law — including laws on the disposition of embryos — and is enforceable by the Attorney General and by private lawsuits against states, with attorney's fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs; states and officials that enforce conflicting rules can be sued.
States would have to add fertility treatment, including IVF, to their Medicaid programs, adding to state health budgets, though the bill allows a delay for states needing legislation.

The bill does not appropriate dedicated funding for the Medicaid expansion beyond the program's normal financing structure, so the added cost lands largely on states and the federal share of Medicaid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it targets — patients facing IVF costs that a single cycle can run to five figures out of pocket — the benefit is large and concrete, and the veteran and military provisions close real gaps in current law. The costs are broad but diffuse: modestly higher premiums, added state Medicaid spending, and federal program costs. The sharpest objection is the breadth of the federal preemption, which overrides state embryo and IVF restrictions outright; supporters wrote that deliberately so patients could not be cut off state by state, while opponents view any limits on embryo regulation as unacceptable. On balance it is a straightforward expansion of a medical benefit whose main costs are financial and whose main fight was over the preemption.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees, later to a health subcommittee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Susan Wild introduced the bill on September 17, 2024, joined by three House Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Connolly, DeLauro, and Larsen.
The same day, it was referred to six House committees: Energy and Commerce, Veterans' Affairs, Armed Services, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, and Oversight and Accountability.
On December 17, 2024, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — its only movement in any committee.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in the action history, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers avoided a new required fertility benefit, and states with restrictions on IVF or embryo handling kept their laws in force. Patients in those states, and anyone whose plan excludes IVF, continue to pay the full cost of treatment out of pocket.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever held; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were House Democrats, and no House Republican cosponsored or advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill creates paying, insurance-covered patients by mandating coverage across private plans, Medicaid, Medicare, and military and federal systems, and protects the right to provide treatment from state restrictions. Clinics' gains come directly from expanding patient access.

The bill forces plans covering maternity care to add a fertility benefit without elevated cost-sharing, a direct claims cost, while also locking private insurance in as the permanent channel through which fertility care is financed. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs opposite to patients' interest in coverage.

The bill gives manufacturers an explicit federal right to make and market fertility drugs and devices free of state impediments, and expanded coverage enlarges their market. Their growth tracks patients' access.

Under the ERISA and tax-code provisions, self-insured and group plans must add fertility coverage, an added benefit cost employers would absorb or pass to workers. Their savings from the bill's failure are the forgone benefit.
